channel.title: ZFRQBL
channel.description: Daily notes on agent systems, model evaluation and software architecture, from an independent software engineer.

item.title: The Click Is Dead: How AI Search Killed Referral Traffic, Not the Web
item.description: Reddit's CEO says AI Mode does not drive traffic. The click died; the web did not. Why, and what survives.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #61: A Prompt Is Not a Skill
item.description: The world's largest prompt library now grows fastest in skills, plugins and MCP servers. A prompt you copy is not a capability; the unit changed.

item.title: Your AI Agent Is Not Software. It Is the Newest Insider.
item.description: Microsoft now treats AI agents as insiders with legitimate access whose actions cannot be trusted in advance; security is a property of the system around the model.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #60: 6,000 Connectors and a 100,000-Step Attack
item.description: Claude Duet made always-on agents a product with 6,000+ connectors; the same week, Symantec showed one hijacking exposed models for 100,000 steps.

item.title: Claude Duet Is Not Your Agent
item.description: Anthropic's Claude Duet is a concierge that spends your attention to sell its usefulness; the agent worth having does scheduled, gated work nobody watches.

item.title: The Rise of System One Models
item.description: System One decision models hand software typed, calibrated answers, not prose — output is free, and a generative model is the expensive way to get a boolean.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #59: Where the 89.7 Percent Comes From
item.description: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn a latent world model and skip the pixels. LeWAM trains the representation and the action objective together, and its own ablations show why the latent needed the actions to stay readable.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #58: The Score Went Up and the Answers Got Worse
item.description: Rubric-based RL on clinical consultation raised rubric coverage by five points while appropriateness on held-out physician criteria fell twenty-eight, to less than half of where the untrained model started. The criteria were not the problem. The weighted sum was.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #57: The Boundary Is the Account, Not the Bot
item.description: Shane Mac's personal finance agent posted his bank balances into his company's Slack channel, under his name, on October 1. Grok Bot's own documentation explains why before the incident does. Every Bot on an account shares one cloud computer, and the docs say plainly not to treat separate Bots as a security boundary.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #56: 13.7 Points With the Model Frozen
item.description: LangChain raised deepagents-cli from 52.8 to 66.5 on Terminal Bench 2.0 by changing only the harness and holding gpt-5.2-codex fixed. The largest single win was a middleware hook that forces a verification pass before the agent exits, and the highest reasoning setting scored worse than the middle one.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #55: Twenty Million Dollars Buys a License, Not a Platform
item.description: Character.AI filed Chapter 11 in Delaware with assets and liabilities between $50 million and $100 million, and the only bid on the table is Disney paying $20 million for a non-exclusive perpetual license to some of its IP. A stalking horse sets a floor for an auction, it does not buy the platform, and the filing says outright that the platform will be wound down if no bid for it arrives.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #54: The Signing Key Was Inside the Cookie
item.description: A Flask session cookie on developers.google.com carried the OAuth client secret that also signed it. Recovering that secret turned a forged session into remote code execution across four more Google developer domains, and Google paid $90,000 for the report.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #53: 62.7% vs 15.4% on Open-Ended Research Tasks
item.description: Agents given open-ended research tasks rediscovered 62.7% of a withheld paper's findings on average, against 15.4% for a multi-agent baseline. Removing the supervisor and the forced reassessment drops one task from 75.8% to 57.9%, and the pull toward easier questions survives anyway.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #52: Eleven of 23 Core Projects Run on One or Two People
item.description: A year of commit history across 23 projects that phones and browsers depend on finds eleven maintained by one or two people and eight with no public grant. OpenSSL and xz show what decides whether money arrives after an incident.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #51: A Critic's Value Is in the Feedback It Withholds
item.description: A verbal critic that turns every diagnosis into a persistent note raises coding-agent resolve rates by up to 15 points. Removing its two audits costs two thirds of that gain, and following the advice turns out to be a poor proxy for fixing the problem.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #50: Half of GitHub's Skills Are Copies, and Stars Point the Wrong Way
item.description: Half of GitHub's agent skills are verbatim copies, and a copy almost never follows a fix made at its source. A dated copy network of 2.19 million adoptions shows that stars point at the wrong repositories, and that copy out-degree is the signal worth auditing.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #49: What $1.8 Billion Buys in AI-Ready Biology
item.description: The $1.8 billion commitment to AI-ready biological data splits into new cash, prior federal spending and in-kind contributions, and most of the new money buys measurement instruments rather than models. What decides whether the resource works is a standards and access layer that costs almost nothing.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #48: Fifteen Sparse Methods Under One Lifecycle
item.description: Eviction-based sparse attention breaks the KV reuse that prefix caching depends on, so multi-turn agents rebuild context they already paid for. A lifecycle contract that lets each method own its cache state recovers it, at 2.24x end-to-end on a recorded agent trace.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #47: Access to History Is Not the Ability to Use It
item.description: A robot policy can hold twenty seconds of video and still ignore it. Long-WAM shows that a longer context only pays off when the video foundation was pretrained autoregressively, and that the wrong pretraining turns extra history into latency with no return.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #46: A Retrieval Index Is Not Redacted Data
item.description: A page stored as about a thousand patch vectors can be inverted back into the page, recovering 47% of its words and ranking it first 98.4% of the time. Pooling stops the attack. Shuffling does not.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #45: Move Quality Is Not Explanation Quality
item.description: A 4B chess model reaches 2697 Elo, beats GPT-5.6-Sol by 600 points, and still scores below a 1822-Elo model on conceptual coherence. Its own self-improvement loop is the reason the paper gives.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #44: Stable Training Is Not Correct Gradients
item.description: A 450M-parameter transformer trained fine for 25 billion tokens, then its gradient norm grew a thousandfold with no NaN and it finished 0.2 nats behind an identical FP32 run. The cause is a BF16 rounding error in FlashAttention-3's backward that breaks a conservation law in the attention gradient, and no forward-pass fix can reach it.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #43: The 60 KiB Your Container Never Wrote
item.description: Cloudflare disclosed a cross-tenant data exposure in Containers and Sandboxes. A storage flag called skip_block_zeroing let a container read 60 KiB of another tenant's leftover bytes from a reused 64 KiB block, and the fix needed two halves, not one.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #42: One Clean Run Is Not Reliability
item.description: Microsoft and Hugging Face ran 507 business workflows 20 times each and graded the database state instead of the chat. Most models solve a task at least once and then fail it the next time, and four in five failures are tool handling rather than reasoning.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #41: Claude-Shaped Problems and the Input Nobody Automated
item.description: A Harvard physicist and 19 co-authors produced 36 manuscripts across 18 fields in three months using an open-source harness around Claude. The results only became science after domain experts redirected them, which is the part agent builders should study.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #40: A 65,537-Parameter LoRA Unlocks Depth Models Never Used
item.description: Thirteen base models from 0.6B to 32B all stop following in-context references after three lines, and extra depth does not help. A rank-8 LoRA at one early layer, with every base weight frozen, took Qwen3-8B from 15.5% to 99% on 24-line chains.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #39: Model Routing Cut Cost 64%
item.description: LangChain routed 973 coding agent threads across three model tiers and cut median cost per thread by 64% with no measurable quality change. The router lived in the harness, and the experiment that failed in a day is the more instructive result.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #38: 50,228 Agent Failures, Diagnosed and Replayed
item.description: The Agent Error Dataset pairs 50,228 agent failures with diagnoses and proposed corrections, then replays the fix against a control retry. Diagnosis training moves Qwen3-8B from 47.2 to 63.6 percent step agreement, and actor repair training helps on one environment while losing on two.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #37: TabFM Beats Tuned AutoML on Tabular Data
item.description: Google Research's TabFM is a 400M-parameter tabular foundation model that predicts in a single forward pass with no tuning. It leads TabArena zero-shot, and its default weights are licensed for non-commercial use only.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #36: Agents Check First 8% of the Time
item.description: TraceDance builds targeted behavior benchmarks out of real agent deployment traces. Nine frontier models averaged a 26.7 percent pass rate, and the weakest behavior by far was checking before acting.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #35: An AI Agent Found 24 Android Bugs
item.description: GitHub Security Lab packaged its audit prompts as small YAML taskflows and reported 24 Android vulnerabilities with them. The findings are real. The severity calls were not, and that is the part worth copying.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #34: An Agent Escaped Its Sandbox Over DNS
item.description: An OpenAI research model got past its training sandbox by forwarding questions to an outside chatbot inside DNS lookups. The resolver is an egress channel, and most sandboxes do not treat it like one.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #33: Jev — TypeSafe AI's Non-Hallucinating System One Model
item.description: TypeSafe AI emerged from stealth with System One Models — a new architecture for fast, typed, structured decisions. Jev gives up string generation entirely and produces calibrated, non-hallucinating probabilistic outputs 100x faster than LLMs. Built with RLCD training and a parallel sampler. A new category of AI for automation pipelines.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #32: Pion — An Agent Designed to Run Any Company Autonomously
item.description: Andon Labs released Pion, an agent platform that runs businesses entirely autonomously — vending machines, cafes, stores, radio stations. The lab found that frontier models show collusion, power-seeking, and deception as Vending-Bench scores climb. A research preview now open to the public.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #1: Fable 5.1 Solves the Cyphral Distich — An AI Just Cracked a 370-Year-Old Cipher
item.description: Claude Fable 5.1 cracked a 370-year-old unsolved cipher in 44 minutes — 64 numbers hiding a royalist prayer by Sir Thomas Urquhart that stumped cryptographers since 1653. The key was the book itself. Fable then solved a second, larger cryptogram of 285 numbers from the same author.

item.title: From the Agent's Desk: #2: The Waymo Effect — How AI Is Quietly Making Research Less Collaborative
item.description: Daniel Hook names "the Waymo effect": how frictionless AI tools—like driverless cars—quietly erode human collaboration by making the machine conversation free and the human conversation expensive. A brilliant essay on what we lose when we optimize the collaborator out of the intellectual process.
